BILL NUMBER:  S3255

 TITLE OF BILL :

An act to amend the public health law, in relation to birth
certificates for children born in foreign countries; and registration
for the adoption information registry; and repealing certain
provisions of such law relating thereto


 PURPOSE :

This bill: (1) centralizes within the Department of Health (DOH)
procedures for the filing and issuance of birth certificates for
children adopted in foreign countries; (2) cures a technical statutory
flaw that prevents the release of identifying information to
consenting parties under the Adoption Information Registry or the
Mutual Consent Voluntary Adoption Registry if both birth parents have
not registered and consented to such release; and (3) eliminates the
access of the biological siblings of adoptees to non-identifying
information available through the registries.

 SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS :

Section 1 of the bill amends Public Health Law (PHL) § 4138-b to
conform the issuance of birth certificates for individuals adopted in
other countries to the manner in which birth certificates are issued
for births that occur in New York State. The bill provides that the
birth certificate will be filed by the Commissioner of Health when
there is no other birth record (other than in the country of birth)
for the individual. The bill also provides that such birth
certificates will be filed only for children that were under the age
of 18 at the time of the adoption, and requires that the adoptive
parent be a resident of New York at the time of the adoption.

Section 2 of the bill amends PHL § 4138··c to replace the term "each
parent" with "either parent" and clarify that identifying information
can be provided about and to consenting parties registered with. the
Adoption Information Registry. In addition, § 2 of the bill eliminates
the ability of biological siblings to access non-identifying
information through the registry.

Section 3 of the bill repeals PHL § 4138-c(9).

Section 4 of the bill amends PHL § 4138-d to replace the term "each
parent" with "either parent" and clarify that identifying information
can be shared among consenting parties registered with the Mutual
Consent Voluntary Adoption Information Registry. Section 4 of the bill
also eliminates the ability of biological siblings to access
non-identifying information through such registry.

Section 5 of the bill repeals PHL § 4138-d(9).

Section 6 of the bill provides that the bill would take effect
immediately.

 EXISTING LAW ::

A. Foreign Adoptions

Domestic Relations Law § 111-c provides that a final judgment of
adoption granted in a foreign nation shall have the same force and
effect as a judgment of adoption entered by a New York court, as long
as either adopting parent is a resident of New York, and the validity
of the foreign adoption has been verified by the issuance of an IR-3

immigrant visa for the child by the United States Citizenship and
Immigration Services.

PHL § 4137 provides that a registrar who receives a certificate of
birth for filing shall furnish a copy to the child's parents or
guardian within ten days and without charge.

PHL § 4138-a provides that the Commissioner of Health will issue a
"Certificate of Birth Data" when presented with proof that a person
who is under the age of 18 and born outside of the United States has
been validly adopted by residents of this State pursuant to a
judgment, order, or decree of adoption issued by a court of competent
jurisdiction in this state, another state, or a foreign country.

PHL § 4138-b provides that whenever a foreign adoption recognized
pursuant to Domestic Relations Law § 111-c is reported to a local
registrar, the registrar shall issue a birth certificate for the
child. The birth certificate will be issued and filed upon receipt of:
(1) proof that the adoptive parent or child is a resident of this
state; (2) a copy of the adoption documents of the jurisdiction or
country in which the child was adopted; (3) a certified translation of
the foreign adoption documents, evidence of the date and place of the
child's birth; and (4) evidence of IR-3 immigrant visa status, or a
successor immigrant visa status. The birth certificate shall include
the child's name, sex, date of birth, time of birth, place of birth,
mother's maiden name, and father's name.

PHL § 4173 authorizes a local registrar to issue certified copies or
certified transcripts of birth certificates upon request of an
individual, if he or she is at least 18 years old, or upon the request
of an individual's parent or legal representative. Because births are
registered in the locality where they occurred pursuant to PHL § 4130,
a copy of a birth certificate is not available from any locality other
than where it occurred.

PHL § 4174 authorizes the Commissioner to issue certified copies or
certified transcripts of birth certificates upon request of an
individual, if he or she is at least 18 years old, or upon the request
of an individual's parent or legal representative.

B. Adoption Registries

PHL § 4138-c establishes the Adoption Information Registry within DOH,
permitting an adoptee who is at least 18 years old to access
identifying and non-identifying information about his or her
biological parents or siblings.

PHL § 4138-d authorizes the voluntary agencies involved in private
adoptions to establish a Mutual Consent Voluntary Adoption Registry,
permitting an adoptee who is at least 18 years old to access
identifying and non-identifying information about his or her
biological parents or siblings.

 LEGISLATIVE HISTORY :

This is a new proposal.

 STATEMENT IN SUPPORT :

A.Foreign Adoptions

Chapter 329 of the Laws of 2008 added Domestic Relations Law § 111-c
and PHL § 4138-b to ensure that foreign adoptions are recognized in
New York and New York birth certificates can be obtained by such
adoptees or their parents.

While PHL § 4138-b provides that a birth certificate will be issued by
a local registrar in the case of a foreign adoption, the statute does
not set forth any criteria - such as an adoptive parent's residence at
the time of adoption - that could be used to identify which of the
approximately 1,500 local registrars in New York State would be
authorized to issue a birth certificate in a particular case. As a
result, the statute permits multiple registrars to issue birth
certificates for the same adoptee, which could be used to commit
identity theft or other frauds.  Moreover, the statute effectively
imposes the burden of reviewing foreign adoption papers upon local
registrars, which may not have the resources or expertise for such an
undertaking.

In addition, the statute does not require that birth certificates for
foreign adoptions issued by local registrars be filed with DOH. This
prevents the State from effectively overseeing or assisting local
registrars in the issuance of the certificates. Further, since such
birth certificates are not filed with DOH, an adoptee will be unable
to obtain a copy of his or her birth certificate if he or she does not
know where the original certificate was filed.

In place of the current requirement that local registrars issue and
file birth certificates for foreign adoptions, this bill provides that
the Commissioner shall file birth certificates in such cases. A
certified copy of a birth certificate filed by the Commissioner will
be provided pursuant to PHL § 4137 or, on request, pursuant to PHL §
4174(b).

This will better conform birth certificate procedures for children
born in other counties and adopted by New York State residents to the
birth certificate procedures for children born in New York State. In
addition, it will reduce the opportunity for fraud arising from the
issuance of multiple birth certificates, and will ensure that
foreign-born adopted children will be able to obtain copies of their
birth certificates from DOH. Moreover, centralizing the responsibility
for birth certificates for adoptees born in other countries within DOH
will spare local registrars the fiscal and administrative burdens of
reviewing immigration documents and creating and maintaining the
necessary birth records.

The bill also imposes several other safeguards to ensure that birth
records are created only when appropriate. In particular, the bill
provides that the Commissioner shall file a birth certificate for an
adoptee h0111 in a foreign country only if there is no birth record
other than in the country of birth for the individual. DOH will
establish policies for the provision of proof that meets such
standards. In addition, the bill provides that birth certificates for
foreign-born individuals will be filed only for children that were
under the age of 18 at the time of the adoption, and requires that an
adoptive parent be a resident of New York at the time of the adoption.
These provisions are consistent with the procedures applicable to
children who are born outside of the United States and obtain a
"Certificate of Birth Data" pursuant to PHL § 4138-a.

B. Adoption Registries

DOH's Adoption Information Registry permits an adoptee who is at least
18 years old to access three types of information about his or her
biological parents or sibling. Identifying information, consisting of
names and current addresses, can be shared only if the adoptee and the
biological parents and siblings are all registered and have consented
to the release of information. Non-identifying information about the
birth parents, such as general appearance, religion, ethnicity, race,
education, and occupation, and the facts and circumstances surrounding
the adoption can be provided to an adoptee or to the adoptee's
biological sibling, even if the birth parents do not register or
consent to the release of information. Medical information can be
provided by the birth parents to the registry at any time after a
child is adopted, and the adoptee can obtain such information if and
when he or she registers.

The Mutual Consent Voluntary Adoption Registry permits private
adoption agencies to carries out the same functions as the Adoption
Information Registry, and permits similar access to information upon
registration and, when appropriate, consent.

Chapter 469 of the Laws of 2007 amended PHL §§ 4138-c and 4138-d to
permit birth parents whose parental rights had been involuntarily
terminated to register with the Adoption Information Registry or the
Mutual Consent Voluntary Adoption Registry and consent to the release
of medical and/or identifying information to adult adoptees. However,
the statutory revisions needed to make this change had the inadvertent
effect of requiring in all cases that both birth parents - if both
have been identified by the court or are listed on the adoptee's birth
certificate -- consent to the release of information. As a result, an
adoptee registered with either registry cannot obtain information from
a consenting birth parent unless the other birth parent has also
registered and consented.

The bill corrects this problem by replacing references to "each birth
parent" with references to "either birth parent" and expressly noting
that identifying information about consenting registrants can be
shared with other consenting registrants. This permits an adoptee, a
biological sibling and a birth parent to obtain identifying
information about each other, even if another birth parent has not
registered with a registry and provided consent to the release of
identifying information. The bill repeals PHL §§ 438-c(9) and
4198-d(9), which currently permits one birth parent to register and
consent when another birth parent is deceased. Because the hill
permits the release of information even if only one parent registers
and consents, these subdivisions are no longer necessary.

Finally, the bill addresses another flaw in the existing statutory
language that allows the biological sibling of an adoptee to have
access to information even if the adoptee is not registered. In most
cases, this would be innocuous, as the biological sibling, who was not
adopted out, is presumably aware of the identity of his or her
parents. However, his or her parents may not wish the sibling to have
access to other non-identifying information included in the registry,
such as the facts and circumstances relating to the nature and cause
of the adoption.  Accordingly, the bill eliminates the ability of
biological siblings to access non-identifying information, and permits
them access only to identifying information which is shared on
consent.

 BUDGET IMPLICATIONS :

This bill is not expected to have a fiscal impact to the State.

 EFFECTIVE DATE :
This bill would take effect immediately.
